---
title: "Calibrating confidence intervals"
subtitle: "Fitting the error model and checking its coverage"
---

The theory is on the [confidence interval calibration](../methods/confidence-intervals.qmd)
page. This one is the practical path.

## The data you need

Confidence interval calibration needs controls with **known true effect sizes**
— negative controls at `trueLogRr = 0` and positive controls at known non-zero
values. The `southworthReplication` dataset is a replication of a
dabigatran/warfarin study with synthetic positive controls at relative risks of
1.5, 2 and 4:

```{python}
import numpy as np
import empiricalcalibration as ec

data = ec.datasets.southworthReplication()
controls = data[data.trueLogRr.notna()]

print(controls.groupby("trueLogRr").size().rename("n").to_frame().T)
controls.head()
```

Rows where `trueLogRr` is missing are the outcomes of interest — the ones whose
true effect you do not know, and the reason for the whole exercise.

## Fit the error model

```{python}
model = ec.fitSystematicErrorModel(
    controls.logRr, controls.seLogRr, controls.trueLogRr
)
print(model)
```

The four parameters are `meanIntercept` ($\mu_0$), `meanSlope` ($\mu_1$),
`sdIntercept` ($\sigma_0$) and `sdSlope` ($\sigma_1$), giving

$$\mu(\beta) = \mu_0 + \mu_1\beta, \qquad \sigma(\beta) = \sigma_0 + \sigma_1|\beta|.$$

```{python}
print(f"bias at the null:              {model[0]:+.3f}")
print(f"bias scaling with true effect: {model[1]:.3f}"
      f"{'  (< 1: real effects are shrunk toward the null)' if model[1] < 1 else ''}")
print(f"heterogeneity at the null:     {model[2]:.3f}")
print(f"heterogeneity growth:          {model[3]:+.3f}")
```

Add `estimateCovarianceMatrix=True` for parameter uncertainty:

```{python}
model_ci = ec.fitSystematicErrorModel(
    controls.logRr, controls.seLogRr, controls.trueLogRr,
    estimateCovarianceMatrix=True,
)
import pandas as pd
pd.DataFrame({
    "estimate": np.asarray(model_ci),
    "lb95": model_ci.attributes["LB95CI"],
    "ub95": model_ci.attributes["UB95CI"],
}, index=model_ci.names).round(3)
```

## Calibrate

```{python}
outcomes = data[data.trueLogRr.isna()].head(6)

ci = ec.calibrateConfidenceInterval(outcomes.logRr, outcomes.seLogRr, model)
trad = ec.computeTraditionalCi(outcomes.logRr, outcomes.seLogRr)

pd.DataFrame({
    "outcome": outcomes.outcomeName.values,
    "rr": trad.rr.round(2).values,
    "ci95": [f"{l:.2f}-{u:.2f}" for l, u in zip(trad.lb, trad.ub)],
    "rr_cal": np.exp(ci.logRr).round(2).values,
    "ci95_cal": [f"{np.exp(l):.2f}-{np.exp(u):.2f}"
                 for l, u in zip(ci.logLb95Rr, ci.logUb95Rr)],
})
```

Calibrated intervals are wider — sometimes much wider — and shifted. Both
reflect measured properties of the design.

Other widths are available:

```{python}
ec.calibrateConfidenceInterval(outcomes.logRr.iloc[:1], outcomes.seLogRr.iloc[:1],
                               model, ciWidth=0.99).round(3)
```

The returned `seLogRr` is back-derived from the bounds so that the calibrated
estimate can be fed into downstream code (meta-analysis, forest plots) that
expects an estimate-and-standard-error pair.

## Check the coverage

This is the step that is easy to skip and should not be. `evaluateCiCalibration`
refits the error model leaving each control out, calibrates that control against
the held-out model, and tabulates coverage across interval widths.

```{python}
ec.set_seed(1)
evaluation = ec.evaluateCiCalibration(
    controls.logRr, controls.seLogRr, controls.trueLogRr
)
evaluation.head()
```

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Coverage against nominal width, by true effect size. Traditional intervals fall well below the diagonal; calibrated intervals track it."
fig = ec.plotCiCoverage(evaluation=evaluation)
```

```{python}
at95 = evaluation[np.isclose(evaluation.ciWidth, 0.95)]
at95[["Confidence interval calculation", "trueRr", "coverage"]].round(3)
```

::: {.callout-important}
## `crossValidationGroup` when positive controls are synthetic

Synthetic positive controls are built by injecting outcomes into a negative
control, so a positive control and its parent negative control share confounding
structure — they are not independent. Leave-one-out that drops only one of them
leaks information and flatters the coverage estimate.

Pass `crossValidationGroup` to make them drop together, one value per group:

```python
evaluation = ec.evaluateCiCalibration(
    logRr, seLogRr, trueLogRr,
    crossValidationGroup=parentNegativeControlId,
)
```
:::

## Without positive controls

`convertNullToErrorModel` builds a model from negative controls alone by
assuming $\mu_1 = 1$ and $\sigma_1 = 0$ — that the error distribution is the
same at every true effect size.

```{python}
negatives = controls[controls.trueLogRr == 0]
null = ec.fitNull(negatives.logRr, negatives.seLogRr)
assumed = ec.convertNullToErrorModel(null)

print("assumed: ", np.asarray(assumed).round(3))
print("fitted:  ", np.asarray(model).round(3))
```

Compare `meanSlope`: assumed 1.00 against the fitted value above. The fitted
design shrinks real effects toward the null; assuming it does not produces
intervals that are too narrow. If you must use the assumed model, say so, and
treat the intervals as a lower bound on the true uncertainty.

You can supply your own slopes if you have external reason to:

```python
ec.convertNullToErrorModel(null, meanSlope=0.9, sdSlope=0.05)
```

## Visual diagnostics

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "The fitted error model: mean systematic error against true effect size, with a plus/minus one standard deviation band, and capped bars showing the null fitted separately at each true effect size."
fig = ec.plotErrorModel(controls.logRr, controls.seLogRr, controls.trueLogRr)
```

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Calibrated versus uncalibrated intervals for the controls, by true effect size."
fig = ec.plotCiCalibration(evaluation=evaluation)
```
